questions.question: According to C. S. Peirce's pragmatic maxim as formulated in 'How to Make Our Ideas Clear,' how is the clarity or meaning of an intellectual concept established?
options: By deducing its logical necessity from a set of foundational, self-evident axioms.
By considering the conceivable practical effects that the object of the concept might have.
By demonstrating that the concept directly corresponds to an unobservable noumenal reality.
By analyzing the linguistic syntax used to express the concept within a formal language.

questions.question: Frank Jackson's famous 'Knowledge Argument' involving Mary, the brilliant color scientist confined to a black-and-white room, is primarily intended to refute which metaphysical view?
options: Physicalism
Epiphenomenalism
Dualism
Idealism

questions.question: In Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz's Rationalist metaphysics, how do simple, indivisible substances ('monads') interact causally with one another?
options: They collide and transfer momentum through direct spatial contact.
They causally affect one another via divine physical intervention on every individual occasion.
They do not genuinely interact; their synchronized changes are due to a pre-established harmony.
They interact continuously through a single, shared universal mind while remaining spatially distinct.

questions.question: In the foundational Stoic text the Enchiridion, Epictetus opens by establishing a fundamental dichotomy that serves as the basis for Stoic ethics. What is this dichotomy?
options: The division between theoretical wisdom (theoria) and practical action (praxis).
The division between duties owed to the state and duties owed to the cosmos.
The division between sensory pleasure (hedone) and rational satisfaction (eudaimonia).
The division between things that are up to us (eph' hemin) and things that are not up to us (ouk eph' hemin).

questions.question: In J. M. E. McTaggart's influential paper 'The Unreality of Time,' how is the 'B-series' distinguished from the 'A-series'?
options: The B-series orders events by subjective temporal experience, while the A-series orders events by objective physical clock-time.
The B-series models time as continuous and infinite, while the A-series models time as discrete and finite.

The B-series orders events according to permanent relations of 'earlier than' and 'later than,' while the A-series orders events according to changing determinations of 'past,' 'present,' and 'future.'
The B-series allows for directional temporal flow and causal asymmetry, while the A-series treats time as an unchanging four-dimensional block.
